newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: U.S. says Jakarta should dismantle car programme.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Jakarta should dismantle car programme.

text.p: U.S. Deputy Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang said on Wednesday Indonesia should "unwind" a controversial national car programme which has drawn strong complaints from both Washington and Tokyo.
Lang told a news conference in Singapore the United States is concerned about the programme and that he would fly to Jakarta later this week to discuss the issue.
"The easy solution is to unwind the programme, but I'm not sure that's the solution Jakarta has in mind," Lang said.

Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry announced earlier on Wednesday that it planned to file a complaint with the WTO over the issue "within a week or so". But Tokyo ruled out using trade or aid retaliation measures as a way to settle the dispute.

Industry sources in Japan say Japanese carmakers currently enjoy a 95 percent share of the Indonesian vehicle market through joint-venture assembly and licensing arrangements with local firms and view the national car project as a threat to their near monopoly.
On Tuesday Washington also warned it would complain to the WTO and said the car issue may trigger a probe under Section 301 of U.S. trade law which allows retaliation against unfair trade practices.
Indonesian Trade and Industry Minister Tunky Ariwibowo responded that Jakarta was ready to face the WTO and argue its case.
Under Jakarta's car policy, a firm controlled by Hutomo Mandala Putra, President Suharto's youngest son, received tax breaks to manufacture sedans in a partnership with South Korea's Kia Motors.
The company, PT Timor Putra Nasional, was the only company granted this privilege.
It must raise local content to 60 percent within three years but has been allowed to import a batch of cars from South Korea duty free, the first of which arrived in Indonesia last month.
Tokyo claims the special tax break violates WTO rules and puts rival manufacturers at a disadvantage.

Lang said Washington was looking forward to the WTO trade ministers' conference in Singapore this December. He said progress should be made on an information technology pact and a telecommunications services agreement.
